T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently avoid Gühring due to perceived high cost and lack of consumer-friendly branding. If Gühring offers a lower-priced, easy-to-purchase line with clear DIY applications, they will switch from generic or competitor brands.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Gühring would sell directly to consumers through an online shop or retail partners, capturing higher margins than B2B sales while leveraging existing manufacturing capacity.
assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops are willing to pay a premium for quality but are deterred by high prices and lack of consumer-friendly channels.
Gühring can adapt its existing tools (e.g., drills, cutters) to meet hobbyist needs without major redesign.
A consumer brand or clear DIY messaging will differentiate Gühring from competitors in the hobbyist market.
predictions: If Gühring launches a consumer line with clear DIY messaging and affordable pricing, purchase intent among hobbyists will increase compared to a control group.
Sales through direct-to-consumer channels will grow faster than B2B sales in the first year, indicating successful capture of the hobbyist segment.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-GUEHRING-UPDATE concerns a durability guarantee for a specific nozzle, not a broader consumer proposition. result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

The evidence remains neutral and does not change the theory.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether Krones AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B product lines, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.

frame.objective: Determine whether U.I. Lapp GmbH should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial B2B focus, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home automation, automotive aftermarket, or consumer electronics).
2) Expand the existing industrial proposition into adjacent B2B segments (e.g., healthcare, renewable energy, or advanced robotics) without creating a distinct consumer offering.
3) Maintain the current business model and not pursue any expansion, focusing exclusively on industrial customers.
4) License or partner with consumer brands to embed Lapp components in consumer products, leveraging existing manufacturing capacity.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Lapp components for home automation if they perceive them as premium, reliable, and integrated into smart ecosystems, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.
T1.who_benefits: End‑consumer homeowners seeking integrated smart home solutions; Lapp benefits by commanding premium pricing and building brand loyalty.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from generic cables to integrated, brand‑trusted components when the total cost of ownership (TCO) is perceived as lower due to reliability, warranty, and ecosystem compatibility.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Lapp captures value through higher margin sales of integrated kits, subscription services for software updates, and data‑driven services that leverage consumer data.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for brand trust and reliability in smart home components.
Lapp can design and manufacture integrated kits that fit major smart home platforms (e.g., Apple HomeKit, Google Nest).
Distribution channels (e.g., online retailers, specialty stores) will stock Lapp kits if they meet quality and integration standards.
predictions: In a test offering a Lapp‑branded smart home kit (e.g., power strip with integrated connectors) at a 20% price premium compared to generic alternatives, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15 percentage points higher.
Repeat purchase rate for Lapp kits will be at least 20% within 12 months, indicating consumer willingness to buy multiple integrated products.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt Lapp components for home automation if they perceive them as premium, reliable, and integrated into smart ecosystems, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt Lapp components for home automation primarily because they need reliable, certified safety components for DIY projects, and they trust Lapp's industrial reputation for quality.
T2.who_benefits: DIY homeowners seeking safe, compliant components for home upgrades; Lapp benefits by selling high‑margin safety‑certified kits and expanding its brand into consumer markets.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers choose Lapp when they encounter a project requiring UL, CE, or other safety certifications, because they associate Lapp with industrial reliability and compliance, reducing perceived risk.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Lapp captures value through premium pricing for safety‑certified kits, bulk sales to retailers, and service contracts for compliance updates.
assumptions: DIY consumers prioritize safety certification over brand trust in components.
Lapp can obtain necessary safety certifications for consumer products without major redesign.
Retailers will stock Lapp safety kits if they meet compliance standards.
predictions: In a test offering a Lapp‑branded safety‑certified power strip at a 15% price premium compared to generic alternatives, purchase intent among DIY consumers will be at least 10 percentage points higher.
Repeat purchase rate for Lapp safety kits will be at least 15% within 12 months, indicating consumer willingness to buy multiple safety‑certified products.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home automation, emphasizing safety, reliability, and compatibility with smart‑home standards. Begin with a limited pilot of a branded smart‑plug kit (e.g., Lapp‑Smart) to test demand before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether U.I. Lapp GmbH should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial B2B focus, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home automation, automotive aftermarket, or consumer electronics).
2) Expand the existing industrial proposition into adjacent B2B segments (e.g., healthcare, renewable energy, or advanced robotics) without creating a distinct consumer offering.
3) Maintain the current business model and not pursue any expansion, focusing exclusively on industrial customers.
4) License or partner with consumer brands to embed Lapp components in consumer products, leveraging existing manufacturing capacity.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Lapp components for home automation if they perceive them as safe, reliable, and compliant with smart‑home standards, because safety and interoperability are primary purchase drivers.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and DIY enthusiasts seeking reliable smart‑home components; Lapp benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty in the consumer segment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers trust Lapp's safety and compatibility with popular smart‑home ecosystems (e.g., Zigbee, Z‑Wave), they will purchase Lapp components rather than generic alternatives, willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Lapp would sell branded consumer kits (e.g., smart plugs, connectors) at higher margins than bulk industrial cables, leveraging its existing global distribution and brand reputation to reach consumers.
assumptions: Consumers in target markets (e.g., Germany, US) prioritize safety and compatibility in smart‑home accessories.
Lapp can certify products for major smart‑home platforms without major redesign.
Lapp's current industrial reputation transfers to consumer perception of safety.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for Lapp‑branded smart‑home components compared to unbranded alternatives.
Pilot sales of a consumer‑branded smart‑plug kit will achieve at least 5% of total Lapp annual revenue within 12 weeks of launch.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt Lapp components for home automation if they perceive them as safe, reliable, and compliant with smart‑home standards, because safety and interoperability are primary purchase drivers.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt Lapp components for home automation if they receive bundled smart‑home kits that include Lapp connectors and complementary accessories (e.g., switches, sensors) at a lower total price than buying components separately, because convenience and cost reduce friction.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking affordable, easy‑to‑install smart‑home solutions; Lapp benefits by increasing volume sales and can price bundles modestly above cost, capturing margin.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers see a kit that includes all necessary parts and is priced as a single item, they will purchase it even if they could source components separately, because the bundled convenience reduces decision effort and perceived cost.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Lapp would sell pre‑assembled kits through existing distribution channels, leveraging its global sales network to reach consumers, and would capture margin on the bundled offering while keeping unit prices low.
assumptions: Consumers value convenience and low total price over component compatibility.
Lapp can source compatible accessories at low cost and assemble kits without redesign.
Lapp's existing distribution can reach consumer channels for kits.
predictions: A test offering a bundled kit will achieve at least 10% higher unit volume than selling components separately within the same channel.

Participants indicate whether they would purchase each kit and the maximum price they would pay. The survey also asks about perceived safety/
X1.sample: 400 participants (200 per region), balanced by age, gender, and prior smart home ownership.
X1.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for Lapp-Smart and Generic-Kit, and binary purchase intent (yes/no).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average WTP for Lapp-Smart will be at least 20% higher than for Generic-Kit (e.g., €43.99 vs €39.99). Purchase intent for Lapp-Smart will be at least 15 percentage points higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average WTP for Generic-Kit will be at least 20% lower than for Lapp-Smart (e.g., €39.99 vs €29.99). Purchase intent for Generic-Kit will be at least 15 percentage points higher.

X1.decision_rule: If Lapp-Smart WTP > Generic-Kit WTP by ≥20% AND Lapp-Smart purchase intent > Generic-Kit purchase intent by ≥15%, proceed to develop a consumer-branded smart home kit. If not, maintain focus on industrial B2B.

final.uncertainty: Consumer demand for a branded smart‑home kit; the size of the addressable market; the ability to certify products for major smart‑home platforms without major redesign; and the competitive response from established consumer brands.
would_change_if: If the survey shows Lapp‑Smart WTP below €39.99 or purchase intent below 10%, indicating insufficient consumer pull.

arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are recruited from Germany and the US, demographics matched to typical smart home adopters. Participants indicate whether they would purchase each kit and the maximum price they would pay. The survey also asks about perceived safety/
arguments.sample: 400 participants (200 per region), balanced by age, gender, and prior smart home ownership.
arguments.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for Lapp-Smart and Generic-Kit, and binary purchase intent (yes/no).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average WTP for Lapp-Smart will be at least 20% higher than for Generic-Kit (e.g., €43.99 vs €39.99). Purchase intent for Lapp-Smart will be at least 15 percentage points higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average WTP for Generic-Kit will be at least 20% lower than for Lapp-Smart (e.g., €39.99 vs €29.99). Purchase intent for Generic-Kit will be at least 15 percentage points higher.

arguments.decision_rule: If Lapp-Smart WTP > Generic-Kit WTP by ≥20% AND Lapp-Smart purchase intent > Generic-Kit purchase intent by ≥15%, proceed to develop a consumer-branded smart home kit. If not, maintain focus on industrial B2B.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify MULTIVAC investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food packaging, small‑batch medical supplies) with a new product or service.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or packaging solutions without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B packaging machines and processing equipment for food, medical, pharmaceutical, and industrial producers.

T1.claim: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts will adopt a consumer vacuum sealer if they perceive it as a professional-grade tool that improves food freshness and reduces waste, leading to multiple purchases per household.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to preserve food quality and save money; MULTIVAC benefits by capturing premium pricing and repeat purchases.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing interest in sous vide cooking and bulk food processing creates a demand for reliable, airtight sealing; current chamber sealers are already used by professional chefs and home enthusiasts, signaling quality.
T1.how_value_is_captured: MULTIVAC can price the consumer model at a premium (e.g., €200-€300) and sell accessories (bags, seals) and service contracts, generating recurring revenue.
assumptions: Home users have sufficient disposable income to justify the price.
Marketing can effectively communicate professional-grade performance.
Distribution channels (online, specialty retailers) can reach target consumers.
predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer.
Purchase intent will be higher when described as a professional-grade tool.
Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts will adopt a consumer vacuum sealer if they perceive it as a professional-grade tool that improves food freshness and reduces waste, leading to multiple purchases per household.

T2.who_benefits: Consumers concerned about nutrition retention and waste reduction; MULTIVAC benefits by positioning the product as a sustainable, health‑focused offering and can command premium pricing.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of food waste and nutrient loss drives demand for packaging that maintains freshness and quality; current evidence shows consumers already value vacuum sealing for freshness.
T2.how_value_is_captured: MULTIVAC can market the consumer model as a health‑preserving tool, price it at a premium (e.g., €200‑€300), and sell accessories and subscription services for reusable bags, capturing recurring revenue.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for products that reduce waste.
Marketing can effectively communicate nutrient retention benefits.
Distribution can reach health‑focused consumers (specialty retailers, online health platforms).
predictions: Surveyed health‑conscious consumers will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer marketed on nutrient retention.
Purchase intent will be higher when highlighted as a waste‑reducing solution.
Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months when positioned as health‑focused.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify MULTIVAC investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would support that investment.

Marketing can effectively communicate professional-grade performance.
Distribution channels (online, specialty retailers) can reach target consumers.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home sous vide cooks and bulk food enthusiasts, priced at €200‑€300, emphasizing professional‑grade performance and convenience. Use existing B2B distribution channels (dealers, online) to reach consumers and offer accessories and service contracts for recurring revenue.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify MULTIVAC investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food packaging, small‑batch medical supplies) with a new product or service.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or packaging solutions without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B packaging machines and processing equipment for food, medical, pharmaceutical, and industrial producers.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing interest in sous vide cooking and bulk food processing creates a demand for reliable, airtight sealing; current chamber sealers are already used by professional chefs and home enthusiasts, signaling quality.
T1.how_value_is_captured: MULTIVAC can price the consumer model at a premium (e.g., €200-€300) and sell accessories (bags, seals) and service contracts, generating recurring revenue.
assumptions: Home users have sufficient disposable income to justify the price.
Marketing can effectively communicate professional-grade performance.
Distribution channels (online, specialty retailers) can reach target consumers.
predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer.
Purchase intent will be higher when described as a professional-grade tool.
Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Vacuum Sealer
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a consumer-grade vacuum sealer (price €200, professional-grade features, marketed for home sous vide and bulk food storage). They are asked: 1) Maximum price they would pay; 2) Primary motivation (professional-grade performance vs. health/nutrient retention); 3) Intent to purchase (yes/no).
X1.sample: 200 German adults aged 25-55 who cook at home at least once a week, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Average maximum price willing to pay (EUR) and percentage selecting "health/nutrient retention" as primary motivation.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average maximum price ≥ €220 and ≥ 40% select "professional-grade performance" as primary motivation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average maximum price ≥ €220 and ≥ 40% select "health/nutrient retention" as primary motivation.

X1.decision_rule: If average maximum price ≥ €220 and ≥ 40% health/nutrient motivators → proceed to develop a health‑focused consumer proposition. If not → no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE concerns running costs and purchase decisions, not consumer motivations such as health or professional-grade performance. Therefore it does not affect T1, which predicts demand based on professional-grade performance and price sensitivity.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home sous vide cooks and bulk food enthusiasts, priced at €200‑€300, emphasizing professional‑grade performance and convenience. Use existing B2B distribution channels (dealers, online) to reach consumers and offer accessories and service contracts for recurring revenue.
final.target_customer: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who cook sous vide and process bulk food, aged 25–55, in Germany and nearby markets.
final.value_proposition: A consumer‑grade vacuum sealer that delivers professional‑grade sealing performance, allowing precise temperature control and airtight seals for sous vide and bulk food storage, while leveraging MULTIVAC’s existing B2B distribution and
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (200 participants, €12,000, 10 weeks) to validate maximum price willingness and primary motivation before committing to product development.
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for professional‑grade performance; actual purchase intent versus stated intent; competitive response from existing consumer vacuum sealer brands; and the size of the home‑sous‑vide market.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average maximum price below €200 or fewer than 40% select "professional‑grade performance" as primary motivation, we would reconsider expansion.
If new evidence shows strong health/nutrient motivation and willingness to pay a premium for nutrient retention, we would shift to a health‑focused proposition.

arguments.measure: Average maximum price willing to pay (EUR) and percentage selecting "health/nutrient retention" as primary motivation.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Average maximum price ≥ €220 and ≥ 40% select "health/nutrient retention" as primary motivation.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-RIETER-UPDATE concerns a training-inclusive offer versus a manual-only offer, not consumer demand or willingness to pay for a branded kit. It does not address T1’s core premise that hobbyists will adopt kits if they view spinning as a creative hobby. Therefore T1 remains unchanged.
arguments.new_claim: Consumers will adopt home spinning kits if they view spinning as a creative hobby, and Rieter can capture value by selling branded kits and premium accessories through its own consumer channel.

arguments.recommendation: Run the proposed Home Spinning Kit Purchase Intent Test to measure consumer demand and willingness to pay for a branded kit. If either messaging group meets its respective WTP threshold and its purchase intent exceeds the other by at least 5 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists. If neither meets WTP, abandon consumer expansion.
arguments.target_customer: Individual crafters and hobbyists who have recently taken up crocheting or other fiber crafts and seek creative DIY experiences.
arguments.value_proposition: A branded home spinning kit that simplifies the spinning process, includes easy-to-follow instructions, and can be sold through Rieter’s own consumer channel at a premium price, leveraging the company’s existing documentation and support.
arguments.next_action: Execute the 12‑week online survey test with 500 crafters, randomizing messaging and measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the hobbyist market and their willingness to pay for a branded kit are unknown; the test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows neither messaging group meets the WTP threshold, we would abandon consumer expansion and continue focusing on B2B industrial spinning.

If the test shows the eco‑friendly messaging group meets its WTP threshold and exceeds the creative messaging group by at least 5 percentage points, we would consider a dual‑track approach combining T1 and T2 elements.

frame.objective: Determine whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Kardex’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to find evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a specific consumer use case.
Must consider manufacturing feasibility, regulatory requirements, and potential partner/distribution relationships.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home storage, small‑business inventory management).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., food‑processing, e‑commerce fulfillment) without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion – maintain current product and market focus, monitor consumer trends without investment.
4) License Kardex’s technology to consumer brands or white‑label solutions for consumer markets.

T1.claim: Consumers in small warehouses and home storage will adopt Kardex’s automated storage systems if they perceive a clear cost savings and reduced manual effort, leading them to pay a premium price for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Small warehouse operators and homeowners who need efficient inventory management.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: When the cost of automation equals or exceeds manual storage costs and the system demonstrably increases throughput and reduces labor, consumers will switch from manual to automated solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex captures value through premium pricing for differentiated consumer kits, service contracts, and recurring maintenance fees.
assumptions: Consumers calculate total cost of ownership (TCO) including capital expenditure, operational costs, and potential resale value.
Marketing can effectively communicate TCO savings and operational benefits to target consumers.
Regulatory requirements for safety and compliance are met for consumer-grade systems.
predictions: A test offering a consumer kit at a 20% premium price will achieve at least a 15% conversion rate among target consumers who report manual storage costs above €500 per month.
Surveyed consumers will cite reduced manual effort and improved inventory accuracy as primary drivers of purchase decision.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Kardex’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to find evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a specific consumer use case.
Must consider manufacturing feasibility, regulatory requirements, and potential partner/distribution relationships.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home storage, small‑business inventory management).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., food‑processing, e‑commerce fulfillment) without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion – maintain current product and market focus, monitor consumer trends without investment.
4) License Kardex’s technology to consumer brands or white‑label solutions for consumer markets.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage solutions for home use if they perceive the product as a premium, space‑saving solution that reduces clutter and improves organization, leading them to purchase directly or through retail channels.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners seeking efficient storage for limited space.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view the product as a design‑focused, clutter‑reducing solution rather than a purely industrial tool, they will be willing to pay a premium and buy directly, bypassing B2B channels.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex can capture value by selling consumer‑grade modules at higher margins, leveraging its existing manufacturing capacity, and potentially partnering with retail or e‑commerce platforms to reach end‑users.
assumptions: Consumers in target markets (e.g., urban, small‑apartment dwellers) value space efficiency and design.
Kardex can adapt its existing vertical lift modules to meet consumer‑friendly size and aesthetic requirements.
Retail or online channels will stock and promote the consumer proposition.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 1.5x the price of comparable consumer storage solutions.
Pilot sales through a retail partner will generate at least 50 units within 12 weeks, with repeat purchase rate above 30%.
Social media engagement (e.g., Instagram) for the consumer proposition will exceed B2B engagement by a factor of 2.

assumptions: Consumers in target markets are willing to pay a subscription fee for storage that is comparable to other monthly services.
Kardex can provide efficient installation and service within a subscription framework.
Real‑estate developers or co‑working spaces will integrate the service as a value‑added amenity.
predictions: A pilot subscription offering will achieve at least 30 subscribers within 12 weeks, with a churn rate below 10%.

constraints: Limited public information on Kardex’s current consumer reach and sales channels.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home storage, small‑business inventory management).

X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions and pricing options. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners in Switzerland who report limited storage space and interest in home organization. They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) Premium home storage system (description emphasizing space‑saving, modern design, and price at 1.5x the baseline price of a comparable manual
X1.sample: 200 participants (100 per condition)
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 0‑10 scale ("Would you buy this product?") and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as the maximum price they would pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Condition B, because consumers value premium, space‑saving solutions and are willing to pay more for perceived value.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition A will show lower purchase intent and WTP than Condition B, because consumers prefer subscription service that reduces upfront cost and provides convenience.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home storage, emphasizing premium, space‑saving design and convenience, and validate demand through a controlled survey experiment.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE concerns a rental versus purchase choice for a compact automated storage module, not consumer demand for premium home storage. It does not address T1’s core premise that consumers value premium, space‑saving design and are willing to pay a premium price. Therefore T1 remains unchanged.
arguments.new_claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage solutions for home use if they perceive the system as a premium, space‑saving product that reduces clutter and increases productivity, and if price aligns with perceived value.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home storage, emphasizing premium, space‑saving design and convenience, and validate demand through a controlled survey experiment.
arguments.target_customer: Homeowners in Switzerland and nearby markets who report limited storage space and interest in home organization, particularly tech‑savvy, urban residents.
arguments.value_proposition: A Kardex‑branded automated storage system that combines space‑saving design, proven performance, and a subscription‑based service model to reduce upfront cost and provide ongoing support.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (200 participants, 8 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium‑priced home storage system versus a subscription‑based model.
arguments.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium price for home storage; the size of the addressable market; competitive response from established consumer storage brands; and the feasibility of delivering a subscription‑based service at scale.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the premium offering is at least 10 percentage points higher than for the subscription offering, and willingness to pay is at least 10% higher, confidence in T1 would increase.
If the test shows strong preference for the subscription model (e.g., higher intent and willingness to pay for a lower‑priced offering), T2 would become more plausible.
If no significant difference is observed between the two offerings, the case for either theory would weaken.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts, emphasizing ease of use, affordability, and professional-grade results. Begin with a limited launch of a Sika-branded DIY sealant in select retail channels, using the evidence that Sika already offers a DIY range and that DIY spending remains stable despite pandemic-related shifts.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Sika’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must come from public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Any recommendation must consider Sika’s existing B2B product portfolio and market presence.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or DIY enthusiasts for a specific use case (e.g., home waterproofing, flooring installation).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., professional contractors purchasing for residential projects).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives.
4) License Sika’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Sika’s own consumer brand.

T1.claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher retail margins on consumer‑branded items, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into home improvement retail.
assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.
Retail distribution (e.g., hardware stores, online marketplaces) is accessible and cost‑effective for Sika.
Marketing can effectively communicate ease‑of‑use and professional results to DIY buyers.

result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-SIKA-UPDATE tests whether application difficulty affects purchase choice for a specific DIY sealant. It shows a kit offering a step-by-step guide and smoothing tool achieved higher purchase rate than a cartridge with standard instructions, even when the products were identical. This supports T1’s premise that perceived ease of use drives consumer demand for Sika’s products.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Sika’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must come from public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Any recommendation must consider Sika’s existing B2B product portfolio and market presence.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or DIY enthusiasts for a specific use case (e.g., home waterproofing, flooring installation).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., professional contractors purchasing for residential projects).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives.
4) License Sika’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Sika’s own consumer brand.

T1.claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher retail margins on consumer‑branded items, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into home improvement retail.
assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.
Retail distribution (e.g., hardware stores, online marketplaces) is accessible and cost‑effective for Sika.
Marketing can effectively communicate ease‑of‑use and professional results to DIY buyers.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded DIY sealant at a price comparable to leading store‑brand sealants will achieve higher unit sales and repeat purchase rate among DIY shoppers compared to an identical product sold under a generic brand.
Surveyed DIY consumers will rate Sika’s product as “very easy to use” or “easy to use” at least 60% of the time, indicating perceived ease‑of‑application.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.

T2.claim: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships.
T2.who_benefits: Contractors who work on both residential and commercial projects and value a single supplier for code‑compliant materials.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika offers a consumer‑branded line that meets residential building codes and is compatible with professional‑grade products, contractors can buy a single brand for both types of work, simplifying procurement and reducing inventory costs
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher volume sales to contractors, cross‑selling of professional and consumer lines, and reduced distribution costs by serving both B2B and B2C channels.
assumptions: Contractors are willing to pay a premium for a single brand that meets both professional and residential standards.
Sika can produce consumer‑grade products that meet residential building codes without compromising professional performance.
Contractors are willing to purchase from Sika directly or through existing distribution channels.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded sealant marketed as “professional‑grade for residential use” will achieve higher purchase intent among contractors compared to a generic store‑brand sealant marketed only for residential use.
Surveyed contractors will indicate that they would use Sika’s consumer product for at least 30% of their residential projects, citing code compliance and convenience.
T2.first_claim: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Sika’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must come from public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Any recommendation must consider Sika’s existing B2B product portfolio and market presence.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or DIY enthusiasts for a specific use case (e.g., home waterproofing, flooring installation).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., professional contractors purchasing for residential projects).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives.
4) License Sika’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Sika’s own consumer brand.

T1.claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher retail margins on consumer‑branded items, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into home improvement retail.
assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.
Retail distribution (e.g., hardware stores, online marketplaces) is accessible and cost‑effective for Sika.
Marketing can effectively communicate ease‑of‑use and professional results to DIY buyers.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded DIY sealant at a price comparable to leading store‑brand sealants will achieve higher unit sales and repeat purchase rate among DIY shoppers compared to an identical product sold under a generic brand.
Surveyed DIY consumers will rate Sika’s product as “very easy to use” or “easy to use” at least 60% of the time, indicating perceived ease‑of‑application.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.

T2.claim: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships.
T2.who_benefits: Contractors who work on both residential and commercial projects and value a single supplier for code‑compliant materials.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika offers a consumer‑branded line that meets residential building codes and is compatible with professional‑grade products, contractors can buy a single brand for both types of work, simplifying procurement and reducing inventory costs
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher volume sales to contractors, cross‑selling of professional and consumer lines, and reduced distribution costs by serving both B2B and B2C channels.
assumptions: Contractors are willing to pay a premium for a single brand that meets both professional and residential standards.
Sika can produce consumer‑grade products that meet residential building codes without compromising professional performance.
Contractors are willing to purchase from Sika directly or through existing distribution channels.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded sealant marketed as “professional‑grade for residential use” will achieve higher purchase intent among contractors compared to a generic store‑brand sealant marketed only for residential use.
Surveyed contractors will indicate that they would use Sika’s consumer product for at least 30% of their residential projects, citing code compliance and convenience.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings (reverse vending machines for deposit return systems and sensor-based sorting machines for waste, metal recycling, mining, and food processing).
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to consumers, not just product capability.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential or small‑business deposit return, sold directly to consumers or via retailers.
2) Create a subscription‑based recycling service using TOMRA sensors to collect and sort consumer‑generated waste at home or in buildings.
3) Partner with retailers or housing associations to install TOMRA sensors in public spaces (e.g., shopping malls, office buildings) for consumer‑generated sorting and recycling.
4) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B customers and existing product lines.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a digital refund system for deposit return because they value convenience and immediate financial return, leading to higher participation rates than traditional RVMs.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers gain quick cash reimbursement without visiting a redemption center; TOMRA gains a new revenue stream from transaction fees and data services.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Digital refund apps reduce friction by eliminating travel time and queue waiting, making the return process as easy as taking a photo of the container.
T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value through transaction fees (e.g., a small percentage per refund) and data services (e.g., container recognition, consumer behavior insights).
assumptions: Consumers are willing to use a smartphone app for deposit returns.
Digital refund speed is a primary driver of consumer choice over physical machines.
TOMRA can scale the app to reach a large consumer base with minimal incremental cost.
predictions: In a test offering digital refunds via app vs. RVMs, consumers will return more containers via app (e.g., at least 15% higher return rate).
Surveyed consumers will rate app convenience at least 3 points higher than RVM convenience.
App usage will correlate with higher consumer satisfaction scores.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a digital refund system for deposit return because they value convenience and immediate financial return, leading to higher participation rates than traditional RVMs.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a digital refund system because they trust TOMRA’s technology and brand, leading to higher adoption than competitors without TOMRA’s sensor-based sorting and deposit return history.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers gain confidence in the system’s accuracy and reliability; TOMRA gains brand equity and potential licensing of its sensor technology to other manufacturers.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: TOMRA’s proven track record in reverse vending and sensor-based sorting reduces consumer uncertainty about whether the system will work correctly, making them more willing to try a new digital refund method.
T2.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA can charge licensing fees for its sensor technology, sell data services (e.g., container recognition accuracy), and potentially earn transaction fees if it acts as a platform for third‑party refund providers.
assumptions: Consumers associate TOMRA with reliable deposit return systems.
Brand trust outweighs price differences in a new digital refund format.
TOMRA can scale its sensor technology to new consumer markets without major cost barriers.
predictions: In a test offering a TOMRA‑branded digital refund app vs. a generic competitor app, adoption will be at least 10% higher among consumers who have used a TOMRA RVM before.
Surveyed consumers will rate TOMRA’s brand trust for deposit return at least 2 points higher than a competitor’s.
TOMRA’s sensor accuracy will be cited as a primary reason for choosing the digital refund option in at least 30% of consumer interviews.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings (reverse vending machines for deposit return systems and sensor-based sorting machines for waste, metal recycling, mining, and food processing).
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to consumers, not just product capability.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential or small‑business deposit return, sold directly to consumers or via retailers.
2) Create a subscription‑based recycling service using TOMRA sensors to collect and sort consumer‑generated waste at home or in buildings.
3) Partner with retailers or housing associations to install TOMRA sensors in public spaces (e.g., shopping malls, office buildings) for consumer‑generated sorting and recycling.
4) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B customers and existing product lines.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential deposit return if they receive a digital refund via a mobile app, because this removes friction and aligns with their digital habits.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers gain convenience and immediate financial return; TOMRA gains a new revenue stream and data on consumer recycling behavior.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Digital refunds eliminate the need for physical cash or voucher redemption, making the process faster and more convenient, especially for younger, digitally‑savvy consumers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value through subscription fees for the app, data monetization, and potential partnerships with retailers or housing providers to place machines in public spaces.
assumptions: Consumers trust the app for secure refund processing.
Digital refund mechanism is technically feasible and compliant with local regulations.
There is sufficient consumer awareness and demand to justify the investment.
predictions: A test group receiving digital refunds will show higher return rates compared to a control group receiving cash refunds.
Surveyed consumers will indicate higher willingness to pay for a service that offers instant digital refunds.
App usage will correlate with higher machine utilization in residential buildings.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential deposit return if they receive a digital refund via a mobile app, because this removes friction and aligns with their digital habits.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing recycling service using TOMRA sensors to collect and sort waste at home if they receive a subscription‑based reward (e.g., cash, points, or discounts) for their recycled materials, because this aligns with their desire for easy, reward‑driven recycling.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers gain a convenient, reward‑driven recycling solution; TOMRA gains recurring revenue from subscription fees and data on consumer sorting behavior.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A subscription model removes the need for manual sorting and collection, making recycling effortless and rewarding, which motivates participation, especially among those who already recycle but find current systems cumbersome.
T2.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value through subscription fees, data monetization, and potential partnerships with housing providers or retailers to install sensors in buildings.
assumptions: Consumers trust the service for secure reward processing.
Subscription pricing is attractive enough to overcome inertia.
Sensor technology can accurately sort home‑generated waste at scale.
predictions: A test group receiving subscription rewards will show higher participation rates compared to a control group receiving no rewards.
Surveyed consumers will indicate higher willingness to pay for a service that offers rewards for recycled materials.
Subscription retention will be positively correlated with sensor placement in residential buildings.

result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.
